The argument of the friends, in proof of <reference osisRef="Job.21.20">Job 21:20</reference>, What pleasure can he have from his house (children) when he is dead--</hi>("after him," <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.22">Ec 3:22</reference>).<div eID="gen7224" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7225" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">when the number, &c.--</hi>Or, rather, "What hath he to do with his children?" &c. (so the Hebrew in <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.1">Ec 3:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.6">8:6</reference>). It is therefore necessary that "his eyes should see his and their destruction" (see <reference osisRef="Job.14.21">Job 14:21</reference>).<div eID="gen7225" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7226" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cut off--</hi>rather, when the number of his allotted months is fulfilled (<reference osisRef="Job.14.5">Job 14:5</reference>). From an Arabic word, "arrow," which was used to draw lots with. Hence "arrow"--inevitable destiny [Umbreit]. <div eID="gen7226" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 21. The argument of the friends, in proof of Job 21:20 , What pleasure can he have from his house (children) when he is dead-- ("after him," Ec 3:22 ). when the number, &c.-- Or, rather, "What hath he to do with his children?" &c. (so the Hebrew in Ec 3:1 ; 8:6 ). It is therefore necessary that "his eyes should see his and their destruction" (see Job 14:21 ). cut off-- rather, when the number of his allotted months is fulfilled ( Job 14:5 ). From an Arabic word, "arrow," which was used to draw lots with. Hence "arrow"--inevitable destiny [Umbreit].

Reply of Job, "In all these assertions you try to teach God how He ought to deal with men, rather than prove that He does in fact so deal with them. Experience is against you. God gives prosperity and adversity as it pleases Him, not as man's wisdom would have it, on principles inscrutable to us" (<reference osisRef="Isa.40.13">Is 40:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.11.34">Ro 11:34</reference>).<div eID="gen7227" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7228" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">those ... high--</hi>the high ones, not only angels, but men (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.12-Isa.2.17">Is 2:12-17</reference>). <div eID="gen7228" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 22. Reply of Job, "In all these assertions you try to teach God how He ought to deal with men, rather than prove that He does in fact so deal with them. Experience is against you. God gives prosperity and adversity as it pleases Him, not as man's wisdom would have it, on principles inscrutable to us" ( Is 40:13 ; Ro 11:34 ). those ... high-- the high ones, not only angels, but men ( Is 2:12-17 ).

Job, seeing that the friends will not admit him as an impartial judge, as they consider his calamities prove his guilt, begs them to ask the opinion of travellers (<reference osisRef="Lam.1.12">La 1:12</reference>), who have the experience drawn from observation, and who are no way connected with him. Job opposes this to Bildad (<reference osisRef="Job.8.8">Job 8:8</reference>) and Zophar (<reference osisRef="Job.20.4">Job 20:4</reference>).<div eID="gen7238" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7239" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">tokens--</hi>rather, "intimations" (for example, inscriptions, proverbs, signifying the results of their observation), testimony. Literally, "signs" or proofs in confirmation of the word spoken (<reference osisRef="Isa.7.11">Is 7:11</reference>). <div eID="gen7239" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4924"/><div sID="gen7240" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4924"/>30. Their testimony (referring perhaps to those who had visited the region where Abraham who enjoyed a revelation then lived) is that "the wicked is (now) spared (reserved) against the day of destruction (hereafter)." The Hebrew does not so well agree with [Umbreit] "in the day of destruction." Job does not deny sinners' future punishment, but their punishment in this life. They have their "good things" now. Hereafter, their lot, and that of the godly, shall be reversed (<reference osisRef="Luke.16.25">Lu 16:25</reference>). Job, by the Spirit, often utters truths which solve the difficulty under which he labored. His afflictions mostly clouded his faith, else he would have seen the solution furnished by his own words. This answers the objection, that if he knew of the resurrection in <reference osisRef="Job.19.25">Job 19:25</reference>, and future retribution (<reference osisRef="Job.21.30">Job 21:30</reference>), why did he not draw his reasonings elsewhere from them, which he did not? God's righteous government, however, needs to be vindicated as to this life also, and therefore the Holy Ghost has caused the argument mainly to turn on it at the same time giving glimpses of a future fuller vindication of God's ways.<div eID="gen7240" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7241" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">brought forth--</hi>not "carried away safe" or "escape" (referring to this life), as Umbreit has it.<div eID="gen7241" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7242" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wrath--</hi>literally, "wraths," that is, multiplied and fierce wrath. <div eID="gen7242" type="x-p"/>
